occupancy.rationale: No Georgia occupancy or bed-utilization figure was found from an official source (listed in not_claimed). The 88% default is an operator planning assumption, not a sourced statistic. The 80% conservative case matters most for small homes, where one vacant bed is 4–17% of census. New homes ramp up from a handful of residents, and the generator computes the ramp-up cash deficit. Verify against local referral volume before relying on any occupancy level.

payroll_burden.notes: Payroll taxes of 8.5% = employer FICA at the statutory 7.65% (not separately sourced here; confirm with IRS) plus about 0.85% for Georgia unemployment tax and FUTA. Georgia new employers were reported at a 2.70% SUI rate on a $9,500 wage base [S25]; this was not re-verified and should be confirmed on the Georgia DOL page. FUTA (0.6% on the first $7,000, net of the state credit) is not modeled separately. Experience-rated SUI ranges 0.04%–8.1% (secondary source [S51]). Workers' comp at 6% and benefits at 5% are operator estimates; get a carrier quote. The effective minimum wage is $7.25 (federal; Georgia's $5.15 state rate yields to it) [S24]. Every modeled wage is above $7.25. No Georgia local minimum wage was found; a secondary source says none are allowed [S43], and a higher local wage would raise labor cost.

configurations.label: 6-bed personal care home, 100% private pay
configurations.notes: The smallest common PCH model (Ch. 111-8-62, 2–24 beds). It is priced at the lower $4,395 secondary benchmark (A Place for Mom-based, April 2026 [S44]) rather than the $5,300 CareScout median [S19], because CareScout measures a private one-bedroom unit in an AL community and would overstate revenue for shared rooms in a residential home. A Place for Mom's own Georgia page gives a conflicting $4,752 average. This model assumes the owner is the paid administrator, with one awake caregiver on site 24/7 (1:15 waking, 1:25 non-waking per the PCH rule text retrieved [S32]; a conservative second-staff rule for PCHs was not verified). Per the rules, a PCH may not provide assisted living care without an ALC license [S18]. Results are computed by the generator; expect thin or negative margins at this size because fixed 24/7 labor is spread over six beds.

sections.executive_summary:
Georgia splits licensed residential senior care into two permit types, both regulated by the Department of Community Health (DCH) Healthcare Facility Regulation Division (HFRD). A **personal care home (PCH)** serves two or more unrelated adults and, in practice, runs from 2 to 24 beds under Chapter 111-8-62 [S18][S28][S36]. An **assisted living community (ALC)** is a personal care home serving 25 or more residents that is licensed by DCH to provide assisted living care under Chapter 111-8-63 [S1][S30]. A home licensed only as a PCH may not provide assisted living care [S18]. In both cases a valid DCH permit must be in hand before any resident is admitted [S1][S18].

Most revenue is private pay. CareScout's 2025 Georgia median for an assisted living community is **$5,300/month** ($63,600/yr, about $166/day), measured for a private one-bedroom unit; the national median is $6,200 [S19]. A Place for Mom-based data reported in April 2026 puts Georgia's median at $4,395/month, though that site's own Georgia page shows a conflicting $4,752 average and another 2026 source gives about $4,940, so treat $4,395–$4,940 as a sensitivity band [S44][S56]. Medicaid reaches personal care homes through the Elderly and Disabled Waiver Program (CCSP and SOURCE), whose Alternative Living Services cover 24-hour personal care supervision in licensed PCHs [S10][S11][S12]. Medicaid does not pay room and board. Waiver residents pay the home **$768/month** from their SSI check (effective 1/1/2026 per secondary sources), keeping $226 of the $994 benefit [S13][S15][S48]. CCSP residents also pay an income-based cost share. **No 2026 Medicaid per-diem rate for Alternative Living Services was found in any official source**, so this report does not model Medicaid service revenue or the cost share.

Licensing fees are low but the ALC pathway is heavy. DCH charges a $300 non-refundable application fee, then an annual license fee of $350 (PCH, 2–24 beds), $750 (ALC, 25–50 beds) or $1,500 (ALC, 51+ beds) [S3]. ALC applicants also need an Office of Health Planning Letter of Determination, a CPA financial stability affidavit, fire marshal and electrical inspections, GCHEXS fingerprint checks, and an administrator holding a Board of Long-Term Care Facility Administrators license [S1][S4][S6][S7]. DCH quotes a 30-business-day initial review from submission [S4]. That figure comes from the DCH checklist, not from the rule.

**Bottom line from the model (88% default occupancy, operator assumption).** The **24-bed private-pay PCH** is the only configuration with a healthy margin: about **$17,944/month net (19.3% margin)**, break-even at 67.5% occupancy, first profit in month 7, and about $374,533 of cash needed. The 50-bed ALC nets about $14,773/month (6.3%) but breaks even at 81.5% and needs about $1.44 million. The 30-bed ALC nets only about $2,958/month (2.1%) and breaks even at 85.8%. The 12-bed PCH loses about $509/month, the 24-bed PCH with 25% waiver residents (room and board only) loses about $1,206/month, and the 6-bed PCH loses about $6,369/month and cannot break even even at full occupancy (117% of capacity). Small homes in Georgia only work if the building cost, the owner's pay or the price point differs from the assumptions here. Aide wages use the national median as a proxy; Georgia's wage may be lower, and overtime and relief coverage are not modeled.

### What this report does not claim
- A 2026 Medicaid per-diem, HCPCS code or unit definition for Alternative Living Services.
- Georgia occupancy rates, competitor names, market shares, referral-source breakdowns, or separate counts of licensed PCHs and ALCs.
- Current official CCSP/SOURCE enrollment or waitlist totals, or how many participants live in PCHs/ALCs.
- Insurance or bond minimums, fire marshal/electrical/zoning fees, workers' compensation rates, or commercial rent benchmarks.
- Georgia statewide BLS wages (not confirmed; national medians are used as proxies and the Atlanta group means are unconfirmed).
- Confirmed average staff-to-resident ratios or RN/LPN weekly hours; these are planning assumptions to verify in the current rule.
sections.service_model:
**Who is served.** Georgia personal care homes provide housing, food service and personal services to two or more adults who are not related to the owner or administrator by blood or marriage [S28]. Assisted living communities are PCHs of 25 or more residents that DCH has licensed to provide assisted living care [S1][S55]. A PCH under 25 beds may not provide assisted living care unless it also holds an ALC license [S18].

**Two chapters, one regulator.** DCH's HFRD lists Chapter 111-8-62 for personal care homes and Chapter 111-8-63 for assisted living communities (25 or more residents) [S30]. The legal authority for Chapter 111-8-63 is O.C.G.A. § 31-2-7 and Title 31, Chapter 7 [S1]. HFRD oversees a combined group of licensed settings, listed on an undated DCH page as 2,910 facilities serving roughly 55,000 residents. That figure covers PCHs, ALCs and other categories together [S28].

**How the two models differ in practice.**
- *Size and building:* a PCH is typically a converted house or small building with a 2–24 bed licensed capacity. An ALC is 25+ beds, so it is usually a purpose-built or converted multi-unit building. The licensed capacity appears on the face of the permit, and the community may not serve more residents than that [S1].
- *Administrator:* under 25 beds, the administrator needs an associate's degree, or a GED/high school diploma plus 2 years of licensed PCH or healthcare experience, and must be at least 21 [S18][S31]. At 25+ beds the administrator must hold a Board of Long-Term Care Facility Administrators license, which for PCHs applies within 60 days of hire [S7][S31].
- *Staffing:* ALCs must have at least two staff present at all times when residents are present, with one on each occupied floor [S5]. Average staff-to-resident ratios and RN/LPN hours also apply, but they were not confirmed against the current official rule text, so check Rules 111-8-62 and 111-8-63 before scheduling. The model uses them only as planning assumptions.
- *Memory care:* PCHs and ALCs operating memory care centers must hold a DCH certification [S41]. The certificate costs $200 annually. The ALC packet requires a current ALC permit first; PCHs follow the PCH memory care process [S3][S4].

**Regulatory change.** DCH amended the ALC staffing rule in 2025, implementing a July 2024 statutory change; the exact effective date was not confirmed [S5][S40]. DCH also presented proposed amendments to Chapter 111-8-62 to its Board for initial adoption on 2/13/2025. Whether they were finally adopted, and their effective date, was not verified [S33].
sections.reimbursement:
**How money actually flows.** Georgia assisted living is predominantly private pay. Medicaid is a limited, funding-capped channel for personal care homes.

**1. Private pay.** Residents or families pay the home a monthly fee. The CareScout 2025 Georgia median is $5,300/month for a private one-bedroom unit in an assisted living community (survey July–November 2025), versus $6,200 nationally [S19]. A Place for Mom-based data reported 2026 medians of $4,395/month [S44], and the same site's own Georgia page shows $4,752 [S56]. The gap across sources is large enough that your price must come from local comparables.

**2. Medicaid waiver (Elderly and Disabled Waiver Program).** CCSP and SOURCE sit inside the Elderly and Disabled Waiver Program and serve frail elderly and disabled Georgians who meet a nursing facility level of care [S9][S10]. Under CCSP, Alternative Living Services means state-licensed personal care homes providing 24-hour personal care supervision [S11]. DFCS policy describes it as personal care home placement [S12]. SOURCE also includes personal care home placement [S17]. DCH contracts with Georgia's 12 Area Agencies on Aging (AAAs) to administer CCSP statewide [S11]. The federal waiver is listed with a current expiration of 11/08/2027 [S35].

**3. What Medicaid does not pay.** Medicaid waiver funding does not cover room and board in a personal care home [S13][S48]. The resident pays the home a room-and-board amount. Two secondary sources put that at **$768/month, set by the DHS Division of Aging effective 1/1/2026**, leaving the resident $226 of the $994 SSI benefit [S13][S14][S15]. No primary DHS notice was retrieved.

**4. Eligibility and cost share.** CCSP applicants must meet an income limit equal to 300% of the SSI federal benefit rate, updated each January. A secondary source gives $2,982/month for 2026, and another gives $2,901, so the official DFCS table was not confirmed [S13][S16]. A secondary source gives a $2,000 countable asset limit [S53]. SOURCE eligibility ties to SSI Medicaid criteria, age 65+ or disability, and nursing-home level of care. The official page says SOURCE is available only in certain areas of the state [S39]. CCSP participants may pay an income-based cost share that offsets the state's unpaid share of ALS services [S11][S13].

**5. The Medicaid service payment is unknown.** No official 2026 per-diem or unit rate, code or modifier for Alternative Living Services was retrieved. Whether waiver ALS claims go through fee-for-service or managed care is also unconfirmed. GAMMIS says Georgia Medicaid includes fee-for-service, Georgia Families and Georgia Families 360 [S21], and secondary sources disagree on whether a state-plan personal care benefit exists. **This report therefore models no Medicaid service revenue.** The waiver configuration counts only the $768 room-and-board payment and understates actual revenue by whatever DCH pays for ALS.

**6. Provider requirements if you serve Medicaid.**
- *Enrollment:* GAMMIS states that providers who have not revalidated by July 1, 2026 are suspended, and that retroactive enrollment is not permitted [S21]. The CY2026 federal application fee is $750, charged to institutional providers on initial enrollment, revalidation or new location [S22][S23]. Whether PCH/ALS providers are classed as institutional was not confirmed.
- *EVV:* Georgia's EVV soft go-live was moved to August 31, 2026, and applicable HHCS claims with dates of service on or after September 14, 2026 must be submitted through EVV. The state selected Netsmart's Mobile Caregiver+. For CCSP/SOURCE, personal support services are listed under HCPCS T1019 [S20]. Whether EVV applies to the ALS placement service itself is unverified.

**7. Waitlists and timing.** Admission to CCSP depends on funding appropriated by the legislature [S11]. DCH's guide says there are nearly always people on the waiting lists for the home and community-based waivers [S17]. Eligible applicants are placed on the EDWP waiting list, and AAA screening determines eligibility and urgency of need, which affects placement [S12][S38]. A secondary source says enrollment takes about 2–4 months and that residents can move into the home during the process [S13].
sections.demand:
**Population.** Census QuickFacts shows 16.7% of Georgia residents aged 65 and over (V2025) on a July 1, 2025 population estimate of 11,302,748 [S29]. That is roughly 1.9 million people (simple arithmetic from those two Census figures). A secondary data site reports about 1.76 million aged 65+ in 2024 (15.8%) on a different base [S29]. Both point to a very large older-adult base. Georgia-specific forecasts of assisted living demand were not found.

**Existing supply.** DCH's personal care home program page lists 2,910 licensed facilities serving roughly 55,000 residents in a combined group that includes personal care homes and assisted living communities. It does not separate PCH from ALC counts, and the page is undated [S28]. Georgia occupancy rates, competitor names and market shares were not found and are not claimed.

**Price signal.** Georgia's CareScout monthly median for assisted living ($5,300) sits below the national median ($6,200) [S19]. Nursing home monthly medians in Georgia are $8,821 (semi-private) and $9,429 (private) [S19], which gives private-pay families a cost comparison when weighing assisted living against a nursing home.

**Referral channels.** A breakdown of PCH/ALC admissions by referral source (hospital discharge, physician, AAA, family) was not found. Two channels are documented:
- **Area Agencies on Aging:** the AAA toll-free line (866-552-4464) is the entry point for CCSP/SOURCE assessment and screening [S11][S38].
- **Private families and placement services:** private-pay residents arrive through families, hospital and physician referrals, and placement agencies. This is an operator observation, not a sourced figure.

**Medicaid demand is real but capped.** Georgia's guide says the waiver waiting lists are nearly always populated, so there are more eligible applicants than funded slots [S17]. A 2026 secondary guide says CCSP waitlists run from a few months in rural counties to multiple years in high-demand metro counties [S37]. Official CCSP/SOURCE enrollment and waitlist counts were not retrieved, and secondary slot counts conflict, so none is used. The practical meaning for an operator: waiver demand exists, but filling beds depends on slot release and AAA referral timing, not on marketing.
sections.operations:
**Staffing rules (ALC, 25+ beds), Rule 111-8-63-.09 [S5]**
- At least two on-site direct care staff must be on the premises 24 hours a day whenever residents are present, with at least one on each occupied floor.
- Every staff member needs training within the first 60 days of employment.
- Staff providing hands-on care, including the administrator, need 24 hours of continuing education in the first year and 16 hours annually after that.
- The administrator and each employee need a TB screening and physical exam within 12 months before providing care.
- The rule also sets average staff-to-resident ratios and weekly RN/LPN on-site hours. Those figures were not confirmed against the current official rule text (see not_claimed). Read paragraphs (11) onward of 111-8-63-.09 on the Secretary of State site before you build a schedule. The model includes about 8 RN/LPN hours a week at 30 beds and about 16 at 50 beds as planning assumptions.

**Staffing rules (PCH, 2–24 beds)**
- Staff-to-resident ratios for PCHs under 25 beds come from third-party-hosted rule text [S32] and were not confirmed against the current official Rule 111-8-62. Check them before you finalize a schedule.
- On-site managers and responsible staff persons must be at least 21 [S34]. A person under 18 may work only under direct line-of-sight supervision, and a 17-year-old may work only in a Georgia high school vocational nursing-assistant track. Treat 18 as the safe floor for hands-on care in both ALCs and PCHs. New staff must receive work-related training, including emergency first aid and CPR certification, within the first 60 days [S34].
- Because the PCH two-awake-staff rule was not verified, the 24-bed models are staffed to the ALC floor of two awake aides 24/7 as a conservative choice.

**How the model staffs each size**
- *6-bed PCH:* one awake aide 24/7 (730 hours/month) plus an owner-administrator salary of $54,000. No overtime or relief coverage is modeled. One 24/7 post is about 4.2 FTE of staffed hours, and the owner cannot count as the awake overnight staff while off duty.
- *12-bed PCH:* two aides on days and evenings and one overnight (about 1,217 hours/month) plus the administrator. This is an operator choice for safety.
- *24-bed PCH:* two awake aides 24/7 (about 1,460 hours/month), 1.5 FTE cook, 1 FTE housekeeping, and the administrator.
- *30-bed ALC:* two aides 24/7, an extra 8-hour daytime aide, a medication tech/senior aide for days and evenings, RN/LPN time, cook, housekeeping, a half-time activities coordinator, and a licensed administrator at $70,000 (operator estimate).
- *50-bed ALC:* three aides 24/7, an extra daytime aide, two medication techs on days and evenings, RN/LPN time, cook, 2 FTE housekeeping, activities, and a licensed administrator at $80,000 (operator estimate).

**Required systems and compliance**
- *Background checks:* GCHEXS fingerprint checks for administrators and individual owners with 10%+ interest [S4].
- *Administrator licensing:* Board license for 25+ beds [S6][S7].
- *Fire safety and electrical:* fire marshal and electrical documentation tied to the application [S4]. Recurring monitoring and inspection costs are operator estimates.
- *Care documentation:* an eMAR or care documentation system is modeled as an operator estimate. No Georgia rule mandating a specific system was found.
- *EVV:* only if you serve Medicaid personal support services (T1019). EVV vendor is Netsmart Mobile Caregiver+, mandatory for applicable claims with dates of service on or after September 14, 2026 [S20]. Applicability to the ALS placement service itself is unverified.
- *Inspections:* DCH inspects without notice, and policies and procedures must be available for review [S4].

**Wages.** The effective minimum wage is the federal $7.25; Georgia's state rate is $5.15 and applies to employers of six or more employees, but state law excludes FLSA-covered employment when the federal rate is higher [S24]. A secondary source says no local minimum wages are allowed [S43]. Every modeled wage is well above $7.25. Overtime under the federal FLSA and PTO or sick-relief coverage are not modeled.
sections.market_conditions:
**Price benchmarks**
- CareScout 2025 (survey July–November 2025): Georgia assisted living community median $5,300/month, $63,600/year, about $166/day, for a private one-bedroom unit in an AL community [S19]. National median $6,200/month [S19].
- A Place for Mom-based report (April 2026): Georgia median $4,395/month [S44]; this figure was not confirmed on its source page. A Place for Mom's own Georgia page gives a $4,752 average, and another 2026 source gives about $4,940, so treat the $4,395–$4,940 range as a revenue sensitivity band [S56].
- The two benchmarks fit different products. CareScout fits a unit-style ALC. The lower figure is used for shared-room personal care homes, so the PCH models use $4,395 and the ALC models use $5,300. Both are statewide numbers, not Atlanta-specific.

**Labor market (benchmarks)**
- Home health and personal care aides: national all-industry median $35,800/year, or about $17.21/hour (BLS May 2025) [S47]. The BLS national median for the assisted living industry is $37,060, or about $17.82/hour. A secondary compilation of BLS data lists a lower Georgia median of about $14.07/hour, which was not confirmed on bls.gov. The model uses the $17.21 national figure as a deliberate proxy.
- Registered nurses: national median $97,550/year, about $46.90/hour [S46]. The BLS RN median in nursing and residential care facilities is $84,300 (about $40.53/hour), so the model's RN line is conservative.
- Nursing assistants in assisted living: the model uses $18.98/hour [S45], but that industry figure could not be confirmed. BLS lists nursing assistants at $42,260 nationally.
- Atlanta metro group means used as proxies for cooks, housekeeping and activities staff ($15.37 food preparation and serving; $18.17 personal care and service) could not be re-confirmed. They are broad group figures, not occupation-level wages.
- Georgia statewide OEWS wages and a Georgia LPN wage were not confirmed. Replace the proxies with occupation-level Georgia or Atlanta values before finalizing.

**Employer costs.** Georgia new employers were reported at a 2.70% unemployment tax rate on a $9,500 wage base, or about $256 per worker per year [S25]; this was not re-verified. Experienced employers range from 0.04% to 8.1% per a secondary source [S51]. Workers' compensation loss-cost data for residential care in Georgia was not found.

**Occupancy costs.** FY2026 HUD Fair Market Rents for the Atlanta-Sandy Springs-Roswell HMFA are $1,585 (studio), $1,660 (1BR), $1,820 (2BR), $2,182 (3BR) and $2,605 (4BR) [S27]. A secondary report shows the FY2027 2BR FMR falling to $1,762 [S49]; the official FY2027 schedule was not verified. The model uses FMR as a proxy for building cost: 4BR × 1.15 (about $2,996) for a 6-bed home, or about $499 per bed for PCHs, and the $1,585 studio FMR per bed for ALCs. Commercial rent benchmarks for care facilities were not found. Rents outside metro Atlanta may be lower, and an owner-occupied building changes the economics.

**Trends and watch items**
- DCH amended the ALC staffing rule in 2025; the exact effective date was not confirmed [S5][S40].
- Waiver funding pressure: a secondary report says the federal share of Georgia's Elderly and Disabled Waiver cost fell to about 65% last fiscal year (it was 73% in 2021), which adds state budget pressure on CCSP and SOURCE [S14].
- The status of a proposed state minimum wage increase (SB273) was not confirmed. The federal $7.25 rate is the verified effective rate.
sections.financial_narrative:
**How the P&L is built.** Revenue per resident-month comes from the sourced private-pay rate (and, for the waiver configuration, the $768 resident room-and-board payment). Direct labor is built from the staffing rules and sized per configuration, with payroll taxes at 8.5% (FICA 7.65% plus about 0.85% unemployment taxes), workers' compensation at 6% and benefits at 5% (the last two are operator estimates; get a carrier quote) [S25]. Fixed costs include rent, utilities base load, insurance, license fees, software, accounting and marketing. Rent and utilities are fixed and sized to licensed beds, so vacant beds still cost money. Default occupancy is 88%, with 80% conservative and 95% optimistic. **The 88% is an operator planning assumption, not a sourced statistic**, because no Georgia occupancy data was found.

**Results at 88% occupancy**

| Configuration | Net/month | Margin | Break-even occupancy | First profit month | Cash needed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 24-bed PCH, 100% private pay | $17,944 | 19.3% | 67.5% | Month 7 | $374,533 |
| 50-bed ALC, 100% private pay | $14,773 | 6.3% | 81.5% | Month 12 | $1,438,822 |
| 30-bed ALC, 100% private pay | $2,958 | 2.1% | 85.8% | Month 10 | $766,953 |
| 12-bed PCH, 100% private pay | −$509 | −1.1% | 89.2% | Not reached | $211,239 |
| 24-bed PCH, 75% private + 25% waiver (R&B only) | −$1,206 | −1.6% | 89.8% | Not reached | $468,229 |
| 6-bed PCH, 100% private pay | −$6,369 | −27.4% | 117.1% | Not reached | $311,259 |

Cash needed is the generator's total of startup costs plus the modeled ramp-up deficit.

**What drives each result**
- **Fixed 24/7 labor spread over few beds.** A 6-bed home carries the same overnight coverage as a bigger one on six residents' revenue, which is why it cannot break even even if full (117.1%). The 12-bed home just misses break-even at 89.2% while paying the administrator a $54,000 salary, so an owner-operator who works the role earns about that salary and roughly nothing more.
- **The 24-bed PCH wins on rent and size.** Contribution per filled bed is about $3,650/month ($4,395 less about $745 of per-resident food, utilities, insurance, supplies, repairs, activities and referral costs, derived from the model inputs). Break-even is about 16 of 24 beds (67.5%); at 88% you carry about 21 residents.
- **The ALCs are held back by building cost and compliance staffing.** The ALC models use $1,585 per bed in rent (the studio FMR floor, excluding common areas) versus about $499 per bed for the PCH proxy. That difference, plus a licensed administrator, RN/LPN hours and a higher aide count, outweighs the higher $5,300 rate. The 30-bed ALC needs about 26 of 30 beds filled to break even (85.8%) and would lose money at the 80% conservative occupancy. The 50-bed ALC breaks even at 81.5% (about 41 of 50 beds), so at 80% it would also lose money. It earns more dollars but a thin 6.3% margin, and it needs about $1.44 million of cash.
- **Waiver mix lowers revenue unless the Medicaid service payment is meaningful.** Each waiver resident brings $768 of room and board against $4,395 private. At 25% waiver mix and 88% occupancy that is about 5.3 residents, which cuts net by about $19,150/month versus all-private (the difference between $17,944 and −$1,206). Because no ALS rate was found, **the model is incomplete, not necessarily negative**. For this configuration to break even at 88% the Medicaid ALS payment would need to be about $228 per waiver resident per month (about $7.50/day, derived arithmetic, not a rate); to match all-private, about $3,627 per resident per month. Obtain the actual rate from DCH or the Area Agency on Aging before building a waiver strategy.

**Sensitivities (derived arithmetic on the 24-bed PCH, 88% occupancy)**
- **Price:** each $100 change in the monthly fee moves net by about $2,100/month. The home stays profitable until the fee falls roughly $850 to about $3,545/month, but only if all other assumptions hold.
- **Wage:** paying aides the Atlanta personal care and service mean of $18.17 instead of $17.21 adds about $1,700/month in cost, including payroll burden (derived).
- **Occupancy:** because contribution is about $3,650 per resident, each lost resident costs about the same per month; an 80% census (about 19 residents) still clears break-even at 67.5%.
- **Rent and ownership:** the lease line is a HUD-based proxy at about $499 per bed. Rent well above that erodes the margin quickly, and owning the building removes it. Both are operator-verification items.
- **Revenue benchmark mismatch:** the $4,395 figure is a statewide secondary benchmark. If your market will only pay a materially lower rate for shared rooms, use the price sensitivity above.

**Honest limits.** Rates are statewide while rent and wages lean on Atlanta-area and national data. Georgia has no local minimum wage per a secondary source, but a local labor market with higher pay would raise costs. Many opex lines are operator estimates. No insurance minimum is required by the rules reviewed, but lenders and landlords will require coverage.
sections.risks:
**Regulatory risk**
- Staffing rules changed in May 2025 and DCH proposed further amendments to Chapter 111-8-62 in February 2025. Final adoption and any post-2025 changes to Chapter 111-8-63 were not verified [S5][S33][S40].
- The staffing ratios apply to residents with minimal care needs. Higher-acuity residents require more staff, which raises labor above the model [S5].
- Permits are non-transferable and lapse on ownership change. PCH ownership changes require 30 days' advance written notice (60 days in specified cases) [S2][S18].
- A PCH may not provide assisted living care without an ALC license, so a growing resident acuity can force a license upgrade or discharge decisions [S18].
- Several rule pages were not retrievable or were only mirrored by secondary sources (Cornell LII, third-party hosting). Confirm every rule cite against the current official text.

**Licensing and capital risk**
- ALC applicants need an OHP Letter of Determination and a CPA going-concern affidavit [S1][S4]. CON thresholds were not verified.
- Fire marshal, electrical, water-test, zoning and local business license costs were not verified. Building upgrades to pass inspection are an operator estimate that can run high.
- The ALC path needs about $767,000 (30 beds) to $1.44 million (50 beds) of cash in the model, versus about $375,000 for the 24-bed PCH.

**Financial risk**
- Occupancy of 88% is an operator assumption, not a Georgia statistic. Small homes swing sharply because one vacancy is a large share of census.
- Break-even for the 12-bed home is 89.2%, and the 6-bed home cannot break even even at full census.
- Private-pay benchmarks conflict: $5,300 (CareScout, private one-bedroom in an AL community), $4,395 and $4,752 (A Place for Mom-based) [S19][S44][S56]. Pricing too high slows lease-up; too low breaks the model.
- Rent is a HUD proxy, not a commercial lease.
- Workers' compensation (modeled at 6%) is unsourced, and wages use national medians and Atlanta group means.

**Medicaid and waiver risk**
- No 2026 ALS payment rate was found, so waiver economics are unverified. Waiver admission is funding-limited, waitlists are nearly always populated, and enrollment can take months [S11][S13][S17].
- The federal Elderly and Disabled Waiver is listed with an 11/08/2027 expiration [S35], and a secondary report says the federal share has dropped to about 65%, which increases state budget pressure [S14].
- GAMMIS suspends non-revalidated providers (from July 1, 2026) and does not permit retroactive enrollment [S21]. EVV is mandatory for applicable claims with dates of service on or after September 14, 2026 [S20]. Whether it applies to ALS and whether a $750 institutional fee applies are unconfirmed.
- The $768 room-and-board amount and the $2,982 vs $2,901 income-limit conflict come from secondary sources [S13][S16]. Resident income below the room-and-board amount is a collection risk.
- SOURCE is available only in certain areas per the official page [S39].

**Labor and market risk**
- Aide, nurse and administrator wage data used are national or Atlanta-area proxies. A tight local labor market could force higher pay.
- A higher state or local minimum wage would increase cost; none was verified.
sections.recommendations:
**1. Lead with a 20–24 bed, private-pay personal care home, if you can control the building cost.** In the model, the 24-bed PCH is the only configuration with a double-digit margin: $17,944/month net at 88%, break-even at 67.5% (about 16 residents), first profit in month 7, and about $374,533 of cash needed. It stays below the 25-bed ALC line, avoiding the Board administrator license, the OHP Letter of Determination and the CPA affidavit [S1][S4][S6][S31]. Do not model the 12-bed or 6-bed homes as stand-alone businesses unless the owner is the administrator and accepts that salary as the return, or the building is owned or leased well below about $499 per bed.

**2. Verify the price before you sign a lease.** Collect at least five local comparables for shared and private rooms. The model's $4,395 is a statewide secondary benchmark (other sources show $4,752 and about $4,940), and the model stays profitable until the monthly fee falls by about $850. Do not use the $5,300 CareScout median for shared-room homes; it measures a private one-bedroom unit in an AL community [S19].

**3. Treat the ALC as a capital project, not a starter business.** The 30-bed ALC (2.1% margin, 85.8% break-even) is fragile, and the 50-bed ALC (6.3%, 81.5%, month 12) needs about $1.44 million. Go this route only with owned or well-below-FMR real estate, a pre-built referral pipeline, a licensed administrator in place, and a CPA affidavit you can honestly sign. If you add memory care, the certificate is $200 a year, and the ALC packet requires a current ALC permit first [S3][S4].

**4. Build a waiver strategy only after you learn the ALS rate.** Call DCH Medicaid and your local Area Agency on Aging (866-552-4464) to obtain the current ALS rate, billing code, unit definition, FFS vs managed care routing, the CCSP cost share and EVV applicability [S11][S38]. The model shows that waiver residents, at room and board only, reduce net by about $3,627/month each, so cap waiver beds at a minority share until the ALS payment is confirmed. Enroll through GAMMIS before serving a waiver resident, since retroactive enrollment is not permitted [S21].

**5. Lock down compliance early.**
- Form the LLC and authorize the application through the governing body [S18].
- Clear zoning first [S1].
- For an ALC, obtain the OHP Letter of Determination before submitting [S4].
- Order the fire marshal report (within 12 months), electrical form (within 6 months), water/septic form and any water test (within 6 months) so they fall within the application window [S4].
- Start GCHEXS background checks for the administrator and each 10%+ owner [S4].
- Confirm the PCH-specific application packet and fee payment timing with HFRD at pchprogram.hfrd@dch.ga.gov or hfrd.applicationswaivers@dch.ga.gov, or through the DCH main line at 404-657-5700 [S4][S8].

**6. Staff to the rule, then to acuity.** Confirm the current staff-to-resident ratios and nurse hours in Rules 111-8-62 and 111-8-63 before you build a schedule, and always keep at least two awake staff where you are using the ALC floor, one per occupied floor. Budget extra aide hours for higher-acuity residents, plus overtime and relief coverage. Train within 60 days and track the 24-hour first-year and 16-hour annual continuing education requirements [S5][S34].

**7. Use realistic ramp-up and reserves.** Plan for roughly 7 months to first profit in the 24-bed PCH, and fund the cash shown, not just the licensing fees. Keep at least the modeled cash on hand before opening, because lease-up is the main driver of loss in the first year.

**8. Get quotes for every unsourced cost.** Insurance (no rule minimum found, but landlords and lenders will require coverage), workers' compensation, fire monitoring, eMAR software, local occupational tax and building rent are operator estimates. Replace each with a written quote, and replace the wage proxies with Georgia OEWS occupation-level values, before finalizing the plan.

checklist.task: Choose your license pathway: Personal Care Home (2–24 beds) or Assisted Living Community (25+ beds)
checklist.instructions: Georgia licenses homes serving 2 to 24 residents as personal care homes under Ch. 111-8-62. A personal care home serving 25 or more residents that is licensed to provide assisted living care is an Assisted Living Community (ALC) under Ch. 111-8-63. The pathway sets your administrator rules, staffing floor, application documents and annual fee. The generator's results show the 24-bed private-pay PCH as the most profitable configuration, and 6- and 12-bed homes as thin or negative.

checklist.task: Confirm you will not provide 'assisted living care' under a PCH-only permit
checklist.instructions: A home licensed only as a personal care home must not provide assisted living care unless it holds an assisted living community license. Define your admission criteria and service scope before you apply so your marketing and contracts match the permit you hold.

checklist.task: Read the full current rule text for your chapter before spending money
checklist.instructions: Read Ch. 111-8-63 (ALC) or Ch. 111-8-62 (PCH) on the Georgia Secretary of State rules site. Rule 111-8-63-.09 (staffing and training) was amended effective May 21, 2025. DCH proposed further amendments to 111-8-62 in February 2025, and final adoption was not verified. Check DCH's HFRD laws page for the latest versions. Free; allow a few hours.

checklist.task: Decide whether you will add memory care later
checklist.instructions: A memory care certificate can only be applied for after you hold a current ALC permit. The fee is $200 annually. PCHs and ALCs running memory care centers must hold a DCH-issued certification. Memory care is not in the financial model, so price it separately.
checklist.cite: DCH ALC Application Checklist; Schedule of Licensure Activity Fees

checklist.task: Decide your payer mix (private pay vs. Medicaid waiver) before choosing size and location
checklist.instructions: Georgia Medicaid waivers (CCSP/SOURCE Alternative Living Services) do not pay room and board, and no 2026 per-diem ALS rate was verified. The generator models the waiver mix with room and board only, and it shows a loss at 24 beds. Treat waiver residents as an add-on after you are stable on private pay.
checklist.cite: DCH CCSP fact sheet; Georgia Health Services Network

checklist.task: Form your legal entity (LLC)
checklist.instructions: File Articles of Organization with the Georgia Secretary of State. A secondary source lists $110 ($100 filing + $10 service charge); confirm on the Secretary of State site. The PCH rule says that for an LLC, the governing body authorizes the license application and the LLC serves as licensee. The name on the DCH application must match your filing exactly.

checklist.task: Get an EIN from the IRS
checklist.instructions: Free online at irs.gov, issued the same day. You need it for payroll, banking, GAHLES/Medicaid enrollment and the insurance applications.

checklist.task: Calendar the Georgia LLC annual registration
checklist.instructions: The annual registration is due April 1. A secondary source says $60 all-in ($50 base + $10 service charge), while other secondary sources list $50, so confirm on the Secretary of State site. A $25 late fee is reported if you miss April 1. The same source says Georgia has no LLC franchise tax; confirm with a CPA.
checklist.cite: Georgia Secretary of State annual registration

checklist.task: Disclose all owners holding 10% or more and identify your registered agent
checklist.instructions: Owners with 10% or more of the stock or ownership must be disclosed in the permit application, along with the registered agent. Prepare a cap table and owner identification before you open the GAHLES application. Individual 10%+ owners also need a GCHEXS background check (see Phase 4).

checklist.task: Open a business bank account and set up bookkeeping
checklist.instructions: Use your EIN and Articles. Keep resident funds and personal-needs money separate from operating funds. Model accounting, payroll service and legal at about $400 per month, an operator estimate; verify locally.

checklist.task: Validate private-pay pricing with local comparables
checklist.instructions: CareScout's 2025 Georgia median is $5,300/month ($63,600/yr) for a private one-bedroom unit in an assisted living community (national median $6,200). A Place for Mom-based reporting gives $4,395/month (April 2026), and its own page gives a conflicting $4,752. The model prices small shared-room homes at $4,395. Tour 5–10 competitors in your target county and price against them.

checklist.task: Review demand data for your county
checklist.instructions: Census QuickFacts shows 16.7% of Georgia's 11,302,748 residents (V2025) are age 65+. Pull county-level figures from the same site. No official Georgia occupancy or referral-source data was found, so build your own referral pipeline from hospitals, discharge planners, physicians and Area Agencies on Aging.

checklist.task: Address zoning and location with local officials before leasing or buying
checklist.instructions: The applicant must address local zoning and location requirements with the responsible local officials. Get written zoning confirmation (use permit or occupancy certificate) from the city or county planning office. Fees vary by locality and were not verified.

checklist.task: Check the certificate of need / Letter of Determination requirement for your size
checklist.instructions: The ALC application requires a Letter of Determination approved by the DCH Office of Health Planning (OHP). A secondary source says no CON applies below 25 beds. CON thresholds were not verified against DCH rules, so contact OHP before committing to a site or size.

checklist.task: Budget the building cost realistically
checklist.instructions: The model sizes rent as a fixed cost per licensed bed. It uses the FY2026 HUD Fair Market Rent for Atlanta-Sandy Springs-Roswell: 4BR $2,605 × 1.15 for a 5-bedroom proxy at PCH sizes, and the $1,585 studio FMR per bed for ALCs. These are operator estimates; get actual broker quotes. Vacant beds still cost rent.

checklist.task: Set your licensed capacity from the floor plan
checklist.instructions: A community may not serve more residents than the approved licensed capacity on the face of its permit. Measure resident rooms and common areas accurately, because the application needs a floor plan with window, door, common area and room measurements.

checklist.task: If not on city or county water, schedule a private water test
checklist.instructions: The application requires a private water test when water is not supplied by a city or county system. The test must be dated within 6 months of the application submission date.

checklist.task: Plan life-safety, accessibility and physical plant upgrades
checklist.instructions: Your State Fire Marshal inspection must show no violations and state a capacity load. Budget for alarms, sprinklers or extinguishers, accessibility work and furnishings as in the startup cost lines. All of these are operator estimates; get contractor quotes before signing a lease.

checklist.task: Check whether your locality requires a local occupational tax certificate
checklist.instructions: A secondary source reports local occupational tax certificates at $10 to $1,000+ depending on the locality and calls them nearly universal. Check your city or county schedule. The model uses $40/month for small homes, an operator estimate.

checklist.task: Confirm your administrator meets the rule for your home size
checklist.instructions: For fewer than 25 beds, the administrator needs an associate's degree, or a GED/high school diploma plus 2 years of licensed PCH or healthcare experience, and must be at least 21. For 25+ beds, the administrator must hold a valid Board of Long-Term Care Facility Administrators license, effective within 60 days of hire.

checklist.task: ALC: apply for the administrator license from the State Board of Long-Term Care Facility Administrators
checklist.instructions: The initial application form (dated 11.2022) requires a $100 application fee plus a $10 processing fee payable to the Board. Applicants need at least one year of full-time experience (at least 1,560 hours in the 12 months before applying) plus a board-approved administration program. The fee schedule was not reconfirmed, so verify before paying.

checklist.task: Book a board-approved administrator training program
checklist.instructions: Required by the Board application. Tuition was not verified; the startup cost range of $500–$1,500 is an operator estimate, so confirm with the Board and the course provider.

checklist.task: Complete the administrator's fingerprint-based background check (GCHEXS)
checklist.instructions: The administrator must obtain a satisfactory fingerprint records check determination before serving. Administrators and individual owners with 10%+ ownership complete a fingerprint-based check through GCHEXS, and the determination letter must be dated within 12 months of submission. Fees were not verified.

checklist.task: Get the administrator's TB screening and physical exam
checklist.instructions: The administrator and each employee must have a TB screening and physical exam within 12 months before providing care to residents. Schedule these before the first resident is admitted.

checklist.task: Confirm age requirements for managers and direct care staff
checklist.instructions: On-site managers and direct-care supervisory staff must be at least 21. Non-supervisory staff providing hands-on care must be at least 18 (PCH rule).

checklist.task: Check your own and each owner's eligibility history
checklist.instructions: A pending-license application is reviewed by DCH. Before you apply, review any prior sanctions or license history in your ownership group. The specific disqualifiers for Georgia were not verified in this research, so ask DCH (pchprogram.hfrd@dch.ga.gov) if you have a concern.

checklist.task: Create your GAHLES account and review the application packet
checklist.instructions: ALC applications are filed through DCH's online GAHLES portal at https://gahles.dch.georgia.gov/. Download the current ALC Application Checklist (updated 07/13/26) and use it as your document list. The PCH application documents were not separately retrieved, so confirm them with the PCH Program team.

checklist.task: ALC: obtain the OHP Letter of Determination
checklist.instructions: The initial application requires a Letter of Determination approved by the DCH Office of Health Planning. Request it early and confirm the process with OHP, since the CON rules were not verified.

checklist.task: ALC: obtain the CPA financial stability affidavit
checklist.instructions: The initial application must include an affidavit from a CPA affirming your ability to operate as a going concern for the next two years. Prepare a two-year budget and funding proof first. The $1,500–$3,500 CPA fee in the startup costs is an operator estimate.

checklist.task: Get the State Fire Marshal inspection report
checklist.instructions: The report must show no violations and state the capacity load, and it must be dated within 12 months of the application submission date. Schedule it after any life-safety upgrades. Inspection fees were not verified.

checklist.task: Get the electrical compliance form signed by a Georgia-licensed electrician
checklist.instructions: The form must be dated within 6 months of the application submission date. Time the inspection so it does not expire while you wait on other documents.

checklist.task: Prepare the floor plan and digital photos
checklist.instructions: The permit application needs an accurate floor plan showing windows, doors, common areas and resident room measurements. It also needs digital .jpg photos of the exterior, common areas and a typical resident room.

checklist.task: Assemble the policies and procedures and the Affidavit of Compliance
checklist.instructions: After licensure, communities are subject to unannounced periodic inspections at which the policies and procedures must be available for review. Prepare them before applying. Allow 2–4 weeks, or use a consultant at your own cost.

checklist.task: Submit a complete application with the $300 processing fee
checklist.instructions: DCH will not act on an application until it is complete with all attachments and fees. The new application processing fee is $300, paid upon submission, and it is non-refundable. Submit through GAHLES and keep the contact email current, because status correspondence goes there.
checklist.cite: DCH Schedule of Licensure Activity Fees; DCH ALC Application Checklist

checklist.task: Pay the initial license fee before the permit or license is issued
checklist.instructions: The fee is $350 per year for a PCH of 2–24 beds, $750 per year for an ALC of 25–50 beds, and $1,500 per year for 51+ beds. The initial fee is submitted before license issuance. All licensure fees must be paid in full prior to receiving a permit or license.
checklist.cite: DCH Schedule of Licensure Activity Fees

checklist.task: Plan for DCH's review timeline
checklist.instructions: DCH's checklist states an initial review timeframe of 30 business days from the application submission date, with applications reviewed in order received. This is a DCH checklist figure, not a rule deadline, so it is not a guarantee of issuance. Do not sign a lease that starts rent on a fixed date without a buffer for corrections.

checklist.task: Do not admit any resident until the permit is in hand
checklist.instructions: The governing body must hold a valid DCH permit before admitting any residents (ALC) or operating (PCH). Operating without one risks enforcement and loses referral trust.

checklist.task: Know the permit limits: not transferable, and invalid on ownership change
checklist.instructions: Permits are not transferable from one community or location to another and cease to be valid when ownership changes. If you buy an existing home, plan a new permit application rather than assuming the permit carries over.

checklist.task: Post-permit: keep the permit visible and know the replacement fee
checklist.instructions: A permit replacement costs $50 per request. Keep the original in a controlled place and display the permit as required by DCH.
checklist.cite: DCH Schedule of Licensure Activity Fees

checklist.task: ALC: build a schedule that meets the 2025 staffing rule
checklist.instructions: Average at least 1 awake direct care staff person per 15 residents in waking hours and 1 per 20 in non-waking hours for residents with minimal needs. At least 2 on-site direct care staff must be on the premises 24 hours a day whenever residents are present, with one on each occupied floor. The rule was amended effective May 21, 2025. Higher-acuity residents need more staff.

checklist.task: PCH (under 25 beds): build a schedule to the PCH ratio and verify it against current rule text
checklist.instructions: PCH rule text retrieved from DCH-hosted sources states 1 awake direct care staff per 15 residents in waking hours and 1 per 25 in non-waking hours. The generator conservatively models 1 awake staff 24/7 at 6 and 12 beds and 2 at 24 beds. Verify the current ratio with DCH before you finalize the schedule.

checklist.task: ALC: contract or hire an RN or LPN for the required on-site hours
checklist.instructions: An RN or LPN must be on site at least 8 hours per week for communities of 1–30 residents and 16 hours per week for 31–60 residents. The model uses the national RN median of $46.90/hr as a conservative proxy; no Georgia LPN wage was retrieved.

checklist.task: Set wages and confirm they exceed the minimum wage
checklist.instructions: The effective minimum wage is the federal $7.25, because Georgia's $5.15 state rate yields to it. The model uses $17.21/hr for aides (national median; Atlanta personal care and service group mean is $18.17) and $15.37 for food service and housekeeping proxies. Local wages in Atlanta may be higher, so benchmark against local job postings.
checklist.cite: U.S. DOL State Minimum Wage Laws; BLS Atlanta May 2025

checklist.task: Run background checks on staff before hire
checklist.instructions: Use the DCH GCHEXS process for fingerprint-based checks. The administrator needs a satisfactory determination before serving. Check the packet and PCH rule for who else needs a check. Fees were not verified; model $300–$2,000 up front as an operator estimate.

checklist.task: Deliver initial staff training within 60 days of hire
checklist.instructions: Every staff member must receive training within the first 60 days of employment, including emergency first aid and CPR certification at PCHs. Build a training calendar and a per-employee file that documents completion.

checklist.task: Track continuing education hours
checklist.instructions: Staff providing hands-on care, including the administrator, must complete at least 24 hours of continuing education within the first year of employment. Starting in the second year, they need at least 16 hours of job-related continuing education annually. Keep certificates in each personnel file.

checklist.task: Make sure two fully trained staff are present whenever residents are present (ALC)
checklist.instructions: At least two fully trained staff must be present in the ALC at all times any residents are present, with one on each occupied floor. Schedule new hires so a newly hired person within the 60-day training window is not counted as one of the two.

checklist.task: Register for Georgia unemployment insurance and set up payroll
checklist.instructions: Georgia new employers are assigned a total tax rate of 2.70% on a $9,500 taxable wage base. Experienced-employer rates range from 0.04% to 8.1% per a secondary source. Employer FICA is separate. Register with the Georgia Department of Labor once you hire.

checklist.task: Buy workers' compensation and liability insurance
checklist.instructions: No Georgia insurance or bond minimum for PCH/ALC licensure was found. Landlords, lenders and Medicaid contracts normally require coverage. The model uses a 6% workers' comp load and $100 per resident per month for liability, both operator estimates, so get written quotes from a carrier experienced in senior living.
checklist.cite: Operator estimate; no rule minimum located

checklist.task: Set up an eMAR / care documentation system
checklist.instructions: Required for medication tracking and inspection readiness. The model carries $250/month for small homes and $300–$400/month for ALCs; these are operator estimates, so get vendor quotes. EVV is only a mandate if you bill Medicaid personal support services.

checklist.task: Write resident admission agreements and a rate sheet
checklist.instructions: State your all-inclusive monthly rate, what is included, and any level-of-care pricing. Include discharge terms consistent with your policies and procedures. Have a Georgia attorney review the agreement. Legal cost is an operator estimate.

checklist.task: Set up food service, supplies and transport
checklist.instructions: The model carries $330 per resident per month for food, $60 for supplies, and $300–$500 per month for optional transportation. All are operator estimates; verify with vendors.

checklist.task: Build your referral pipeline before the permit arrives
checklist.instructions: Meet hospital discharge planners, physicians, home health agencies and Area Agencies on Aging. The statewide AAA line is 866-552-4464. The model ramps 1–5 new residents a month depending on size, an operator assumption, so verify against your pipeline.

checklist.task: Plan cash to carry you through ramp-up
checklist.instructions: The generator's cash-needed estimates at default occupancy: 6-bed PCH about $311,259; 12-bed PCH about $211,239; 24-bed PCH about $374,533; 30-bed ALC about $766,953; 50-bed ALC about $1,438,822. The 24-bed private-pay PCH reaches first profit in month 7 and the 50-bed ALC in month 12. The 6-bed and 12-bed PCHs and the waiver mix never reach profit in the model.

checklist.task: Prepare for unannounced periodic inspections
checklist.instructions: Communities are subject to unannounced periodic inspections at which policies and procedures must be available for review. Run internal mock inspections monthly: staffing sheets, training files, TB/physicals, resident files and fire drill logs.

checklist.task: Never exceed licensed capacity
checklist.instructions: Admissions must stay at or under the approved licensed capacity printed on the permit. Track census daily and block admissions when you reach capacity.

checklist.task: Keep DCH contact information current
checklist.instructions: Questions about regulations, surveys, permits and administrator contact updates go to the Personal Care Home Team at pchprogram.hfrd@dch.ga.gov. DCH's phone is (404) 656-4507, and the office is at 2 Martin Luther King Jr. Drive SE, East Tower, Atlanta, GA 30334, Monday–Friday, 8 a.m.–5 p.m. ET.

checklist.task: Market to your target segment with accurate claims
checklist.instructions: Price against local comparables and describe only services your permit allows. A PCH-only permit does not allow assisted living care. Do not advertise memory care until DCH issues the certification.

checklist.phase: PHASE 7 — OPTIONAL: MEDICAID WAIVER (CCSP / SOURCE) PARTICIPATION
checklist.task: Understand how waiver money flows before accepting waiver residents
checklist.instructions: CCSP and SOURCE sit inside the Elderly and Disabled Waiver Program. Alternative Living Services covers 24-hour personal care supervision in state-licensed personal care homes. Medicaid does not pay room and board; the resident pays $768/month (secondary sources, effective 1/1/2026) and keeps $226 of the $994 SSI benefit. No 2026 ALS per-diem rate was verified, so get the rate and billing rules from the waiver program before you commit beds.
checklist.cite: DCH CCSP fact sheet; Georgia Health Services Network

checklist.phase: PHASE 7 — OPTIONAL: MEDICAID WAIVER (CCSP / SOURCE) PARTICIPATION
checklist.task: Learn how residents enter the waiver
checklist.instructions: Entry starts with an assessment requested through the local Area Agency on Aging (866-552-4464). The screening determines eligibility and urgency, which affects the waiting-list position. DFCS determines financial eligibility and keeps the EDWP waiting list. Admission depends on legislative funding, and DCH's guide says waiver waitlists are nearly always populated.
checklist.cite: Georgia.gov EDWP; PAMMS 2131; DCH waiver guide

checklist.phase: PHASE 7 — OPTIONAL: MEDICAID WAIVER (CCSP / SOURCE) PARTICIPATION
checklist.task: Verify current eligibility limits for prospective waiver residents
checklist.instructions: Secondary sources put the 2026 CCSP income limit at 300% of the federal benefit rate ($2,982) or $2,901, and these conflict. The individual asset limit is reported at $2,000 from secondary sources. Confirm with DFCS before telling a family a resident qualifies. SOURCE eligibility ties to SSI Medicaid criteria and nursing facility level of care; Georgia.gov says SOURCE is only available in certain areas.

checklist.phase: PHASE 7 — OPTIONAL: MEDICAID WAIVER (CCSP / SOURCE) PARTICIPATION
checklist.task: Enroll as a Georgia Medicaid provider through GAMMIS before billing
checklist.instructions: Retroactive enrollment is not permitted, so services before enrollment are not payable. GAMMIS also states that providers who had not revalidated by July 1, 2026 are suspended. Start enrollment well before the first waiver admission. Allow several weeks, but no processing time was verified.

checklist.phase: PHASE 7 — OPTIONAL: MEDICAID WAIVER (CCSP / SOURCE) PARTICIPATION
checklist.task: Budget the CY2026 Medicaid provider enrollment application fee, if it applies
checklist.instructions: The CY2026 federal application fee is $750 for institutional providers, charged at initial enrollment, revalidation or a new location. Whether PCH/ALS waiver providers are classed as institutional was not confirmed, so ask GAMMIS before paying. Skip this if you stay private-pay only.
checklist.cite: CMS CY2026 application fee notice; MLN9658742

checklist.phase: PHASE 7 — OPTIONAL: MEDICAID WAIVER (CCSP / SOURCE) PARTICIPATION
checklist.task: Prepare for EVV if you bill personal support services
checklist.instructions: DCH selected Netsmart Mobile Caregiver+ as the state EVV system. For CCSP and SOURCE, personal support services are listed under HCPCS T1019. The EVV soft go-live is August 31, 2026, and applicable HHCS claims with dates of service on or after September 14, 2026 must be submitted through EVV. Whether EVV applies to the ALS placement service itself is unverified, so confirm with DCH.

checklist.phase: PHASE 7 — OPTIONAL: MEDICAID WAIVER (CCSP / SOURCE) PARTICIPATION
checklist.task: Track funding and waiver renewal risk
checklist.instructions: CMS lists the Georgia Elderly and Disabled Waiver as expiring 11/08/2027. A secondary report says the federal share of EDWP costs has fallen to about 65%, which raises state budget pressure. Do not rely on Medicaid revenue in your base-case budget.

checklist.task: Pay the DCH annual license fee on time
checklist.instructions: PCH 2–24 beds: $350 annually; ALC 25–50 beds: $750; ALC 51+ beds: $1,500. A late fee of $150 per instance applies 60 days past due. The model carries the fee as a monthly fixed line.
checklist.cite: DCH Schedule of Licensure Activity Fees

checklist.task: Give required notice before any change of ownership
checklist.instructions: PCH rule: at least 30 days written notice to DCH and all residents of an impending change of ownership (60 days for impending bankruptcy or eviction). Because the permit is invalid on ownership change, the new owner must obtain a permit.

checklist.task: Apply for the memory care certificate only after you hold a current ALC permit
checklist.instructions: Fee: $200 annually. DCH issues the certification, and staffing and training requirements for memory care were not verified, so get them from DCH before you enroll memory care residents. Treat revenue and cost as outside this model.
checklist.cite: DCH ALC Application Checklist; Fee Schedule

checklist.task: Update financial model quarterly against actuals
checklist.instructions: Compare actual census, labor hours and rent against the model. The break-even occupancy per the generator is 67.5% for the 24-bed PCH, 81.5% for the 50-bed ALC, 85.8% for the 30-bed ALC, 89.2% for the 12-bed PCH and 89.8% for the 24-bed waiver mix. If your census is below break-even for 3 months, adjust rates or costs.

checklist.task: Watch for rule changes
checklist.instructions: DCH presented proposed amendments to Ch. 111-8-62 to its Board on 2/13/2025, and final adoption was not verified. Check the HFRD laws page and the Secretary of State rules site each quarter, and subscribe to DCH notices.
checklist.cite: HFRD Laws & Regulations; DCH rule synopsis

checklist.task: Stress-test wages and rent in your metro
checklist.instructions: The modeled aide wage is the national median ($17.21/hr), not a Georgia statewide wage, which could not be retrieved. If your local market pays more, rerun the model. The secondary source says no local minimum wage is allowed in Georgia, but that was not verified against a statute.

checklist.task: Renew business licenses, insurance and annual registration on a calendar
checklist.instructions: Track the LLC annual registration (April 1), the local occupational tax certificate, insurance renewals, the DCH license renewal date, administrator license renewal and staff CE deadlines. Assign one person to own the calendar.
